title: How a four-stroke car engine works

parts.label: Crankcase
parts.brief: A wide, rounded metal box at the bottom of the engine that holds the crankshaft and the oil. It is dark grey cast aluminium with a ribbed oil pan underneath, a row of small bolts around its top edge and a drain plug at the bottom.

parts.label: Crankshaft
parts.brief: A shiny steel shaft running left to right with a zig-zag bend in the middle called a crank throw, plus two heavy half-moon counterweights. Its ends are round polished journals, and a small toothed gear sits on one end.

parts.label: Cylinder
parts.brief: A tall, chunky block of grey cast iron with a smooth round tube bored through its middle, where the piston slides. The outside has cooling channels and fins, and bolt holes at the four top corners.

parts.label: Piston
parts.brief: A short, round silver aluminium cup that slides up and down inside the cylinder, with a flat top. Three thin dark piston rings wrap around its upper side, and a steel pin crosses through its skirt to hold the connecting rod.

parts.label: Connecting rod
parts.brief: A strong steel rod shaped like a long bone, with a small round eye at the top for the piston pin and a big round split end at the bottom that clamps around the crankshaft with two bolts. It is dull grey steel.

parts.label: Cylinder head
parts.brief: A flat, heavy lid of aluminium bolted on top of the cylinder, painted silver with a black valve cover on top. It has two round ports on the sides for the pipes, and a threaded hole in the middle for the spark plug.

parts.label: Intake valve
parts.brief: A thin steel stem with a round mushroom-shaped head at the bottom that opens and closes the air inlet. A coiled spring wraps around the top of the stem. Give it a blue tint so kids can tell it apart from the exhaust valve.

parts.label: Exhaust valve
parts.brief: A thin steel stem with a round mushroom-shaped head at the bottom that opens and closes the exhaust outlet. A coiled spring wraps around its top. Give it a reddish, heat-darkened tint.

parts.label: Spark plug
parts.brief: A small plug standing on top of the head: a white ceramic body with ribs, a six-sided silver nut in the middle and a threaded tip with a tiny metal hook electrode. A black cap with a wire sits on its top.

parts.label: Air intake
parts.brief: A short, round black pipe leading fresh air into the back of the cylinder head, with a flange and two bolts where it joins. A small silver fuel injector nozzle pokes into its side.

parts.label: Exhaust pipe
parts.brief: A short, round metal pipe leading out of the front of the cylinder head, bolted on with a flange. It is rusty brown and heat-blued, like a real exhaust manifold.

steps.say: This is a car engine! It turns lots of tiny bursts of burning fuel into spinning, and that spinning turns the car's wheels.
Let's look inside the cylinder. The piston slides up and down in it, like a plunger in a syringe. It does four moves, called strokes: suck, squeeze, bang, blow!
Stroke one is suck. The intake valve opens and the piston slides down. That pulls air and a little fuel in, just like pulling back a syringe.
Stroke two is squeeze. The valve shuts and the piston pushes back up, squashing the air and fuel into a tiny space, like squeezing a balloon in your fist.
Stroke three is bang! The spark plug makes a tiny spark. The squashed fuel burns in a flash, and the hot gas shoves the piston down hard. This is the stroke that gives the power.
Stroke four is blow. The exhaust valve opens and the piston rises, pushing the used, smoky gas out of the exhaust pipe. Then it starts again!
The connecting rod links the piston to the bendy crankshaft. Up-and-down turns into round-and-round, just like your legs pushing bike pedals in a circle.
Here's the whole engine back together. Most cars have four of these cylinders taking turns, so the crankshaft keeps spinning smoothly!

recap: A car engine repeats four strokes, suck, squeeze, bang, blow, and the crankshaft turns the piston's up-and-down push into spinning.
question: What do you think would happen if the spark plug never sparked?
